title: Why Compression Taps Leak: The Worn Washer
description: When a compression tap drips, forcing the handle tighter feels like an instant fix, but it actually causes more damage. Inside the tap spindle, a rubber washer presses against a smooth brass valve seat to seal off water flow. Over time, friction, heat, and mineral buildup cause the rubber to harden, split, or deform. Forcing a leaking tap tightly closed grinds the compromised rubber directly into the metal seat, which can permanently score the brass body. If your tap drips continuously from the spout, isolate the water supply, disassemble the stem, and inspect the washer. Replacing a cheap rubber seal early preserves the tap body.
image_prompt: A crisp, photorealistic macro close-up photograph of a disassembled brass tap spindle resting on a clean plumber's work surface. The brass stem shows realistic metallic texture and slight water scaling. At the base of the spindle, an old, cracked, and deformed black rubber washer is clearly visible, showing obvious wear and tear. Positioned right beside it is a brand-new, perfectly smooth, round black rubber washer for clear physical comparison. An adjustable spanner rests neatly in the soft-focus background. Clean, bright directional workshop lighting creates realistic reflections on the brass and highlights the rough texture of the damaged rubber. Vertical 9:16 composition, shallow depth of field with main subject centered. No text, no logos, no watermarks, no arrows, no graphics.
visual_story: A macro visual showing a dismantled brass tap spindle with a degraded, split washer placed beside a fresh replacement washer. This visual clearly reveals the mechanical cause of persistent drips to viewers without requiring reading.

on_image_text.explanation: Overtightening grinds down the rubber washer and damages the internal brass seat.
on_image_text.takeaway: Replace worn washers early to prevent permanent damage to the tap body.
